children.text: Healthcare transformation is usually discussed as a problem of policy design: the right payment model, the right mandate, the right technology. Chapter 15 of Transforming Healthcare makes a different argument. Once the design is settled, transformation becomes a problem of delivery, and delivery at this scale is a discipline with its own standards, roles and tools. Most transformation efforts never adopt that discipline, and the gap shows up as missed deadlines, stranded investments and reforms that exist on paper but not in practice.

This opening lesson makes the case that the gap is real and costly. It shows how every concept in the five-pillar framework maps onto a project-management discipline, what the evidence says about the cost of poor delivery, what a well-documented federal health program failure looked like from the inside, and how the same gap appears in Vermont's transformation today.

The rest of the course then builds the discipline step by step: defining the portfolio, staffing and governing it, scheduling it by dependency, managing its risks, tracing its benefits, and making the case for paying for it.
Every Framework Concept Is a Management Discipline

Chapter 15 opens with an observation that reframes the whole book. Every concept introduced in the earlier chapters maps to an established project-management discipline, whether or not it was presented in those terms. Defining the five pillars is scope management: deciding what is in and out of each body of work. The execution sequence is schedule management with dependency logic. The failure cascade, in which a weak upstream pillar degrades everything downstream, is risk management. The implementation matrix is cost and resource management. The Vermont Scorecard is benefits-realization management.

Put those together and the five-pillar framework is, in its entirety, a portfolio-management architecture. The book's diagnosis of Vermont follows directly: the state has the analytical architecture but is not managing its transformation as a portfolio. The analysis exists; the operating machinery to act on it does not.

This matters because analysis and delivery fail differently. A flawed analysis can be corrected by better analysis. A delivery gap cannot: no amount of additional insight will coordinate nineteen components owned by different agencies against a single statutory deadline. That takes people with the authority and the tools to do it.

The five-pillar framework tells you what has to be built and in what order. Portfolio management is the discipline that makes sure it actually gets built in that order, by people accountable for the result.

children.text: What Poor Delivery Costs

The Project Management Institute (PMI) surveys organizations every year on how their projects perform, in a report called Pulse of the Profession. Its 2017 edition put the cost of poor project performance at about 9.7% of project spending: roughly $97 million wasted for every $1 billion invested. The 2018 edition put it at 9.9%. These are cross-industry averages, not healthcare-specific figures, but they set the order of magnitude: a meaningful share of every transformation budget is at risk from how the work is managed, not from what the work is.

The same research program has consistently found large differences between organizations that manage delivery well and those that do not. PMI's 2014 report, The High Cost of Low Performance, found that high-performing organizations completed 89% of their projects successfully against 36% for low performers, and that projects aligned to organizational strategy succeeded more often than misaligned ones. Alignment to strategy is precisely what portfolio management exists to provide.

Treat these figures with appropriate care. They are self-reported survey results, the definitions of success have shifted between editions, and none of them is a forecast for any particular program. Their value is directional: across thousands of organizations, the way work is governed shows up in whether it delivers.

children.text: A Health Case From the Inside: HealthCare.gov

The most thoroughly documented delivery failure in recent American health policy is the October 2013 launch of HealthCare.gov, the federal insurance marketplace created under the Affordable Care Act. Two federal reviews examined what went wrong, and both describe management failures rather than a flawed policy idea.

The Government Accountability Office's July 2014 report, GAO-14-694, found that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) began building the marketplace systems without effective planning or oversight. Task orders were issued while key requirements were still unknown, including how many states would use the federal marketplace and how many people might enroll. Unclear guidance left confusion over who had authority to approve contractor requests to spend funds. Key governance reviews were delayed, and the site launched without verification that it met its performance requirements. The HHS Office of Inspector General's 2016 case study, based on interviews with 86 officials, staff and contractors, reached a similar picture and also recorded the recovery: CMS restored the site for high consumer use within two months and adopted more effective organizational practices.

Every element of that list is a portfolio-management failure. Requirements were not defined before work began. Authority was not assigned. Governance checkpoints were skipped. Nobody verified that the component everything else depended on was ready before the date arrived. The recovery, equally, came from putting integrated management in place, not from changing the policy.

GAO-14-694 found that CMS issued task orders before key technical requirements were known, that unclear guidance caused confusion over who could approve contractor spending, that key governance reviews were delayed, and that the site launched without verification that it met performance requirements.
The HHS Inspector General's case study (OEI-06-14-00350) found that CMS recovered the website for high consumer use within two months and adopted more effective organizational practices, and called on the agency to keep applying those lessons.

body.message: HealthCare.gov is often filed as an IT failure. The federal reviews describe something more general: a program with a fixed public deadline, many contractors and no single point of integrated accountability. That description fits most state health-transformation efforts, whatever their technology content.
body.title: The lesson is not 'technology projects fail'

children.text: Vermont's Version of the Gap

Chapter 15 applies the same lens to Vermont. The Agency of Human Services (AHS) is managing the state's transformation as a collection of projects without the program or portfolio infrastructure to coordinate them, so work is sequenced by who is available rather than by what the portfolio needs. The book is explicit that this is not a criticism of AHS staff, who are executing an extraordinary mandate with insufficient capacity. It is a structural observation: the capacity does not yet exist.

The need was identified early. Oliver Wyman's Act 167 report recommended in 2024 that AHS establish a dedicated project-management function, and the November 2025 transformation report repeated the finding. Chapter 15's contribution is to define that function precisely, using PMI's standards, and to schedule it against the January 15, 2028 deadline for the Statewide Health Care Delivery Strategic Plan.

The scale is what makes the gap dangerous. Chapter 15 counts 19 components in the transformation portfolio, ten scored risks in its register, and fourteen hospital transformation plans the portfolio must coordinate. No component manager, however capable, can see across all of that from inside one component.

children.text: What This Course Covers

The course follows the order in which a portfolio function is actually built. Track 1, which you are in now, establishes the levels of management and how to define a portfolio by inventorying its components. Track 2 staffs and governs it: the Portfolio Manager, the five pillar program managers, the governance tiers and the ten knowledge areas a portfolio office has to run.

Track 3 schedules the portfolio by dependency rather than by deadline, chooses predictive, adaptive or hybrid management for each component, and measures progress with earned value. Track 4 builds and reads the risk register and traces every component to the benefits that justify it. Track 5 makes the business case, answers the standard objections, and ends with a capstone in which you build and run a portfolio of your own on the platform's tools.

Two companion resources sit alongside this course. Five Pillars, One Imperative introduces the portfolio argument in a single Track 8 lesson, and the Transformation Leadership course includes a hands-on workshop on running the sequencing test. This course goes deeper on the management system itself; the workshop is the best place to practise one technique in isolation.

A useful test to carry through the course comes from the chapter's advice to legislators and boards: which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? An organization managing a real portfolio can answer in one sentence.

points: Every concept in the five-pillar framework maps to a project-management discipline: scope, schedule, risk, cost and resources, and benefits realization.
PMI's Pulse of the Profession put waste from poor project performance at about 9.7% of project spending in 2017 and 9.9% in 2018, across industries.
High-performing organizations complete far more projects successfully than low performers, and strategic alignment, the core job of portfolio management, is part of the difference.
GAO found that HealthCare.gov was built without effective planning or oversight: undefined requirements, unclear authority, delayed governance reviews and no verification before launch.
Vermont's transformation is being managed as a collection of projects; Oliver Wyman recommended a project-management function in 2024 and the November 2025 report repeated it.
Vermont's portfolio has 19 components, ten scored risks and fourteen hospital plans converging on the January 15, 2028 Strategic Plan.
The test of a real portfolio is whether its managers can name the binding constraint, its owner and what would accelerate it in one sentence.

body.explanation: GAO-14-694 describes management failures: task orders issued while key requirements were unknown, confusion over who could approve contractor spending, delayed governance reviews, and a launch without verification against performance requirements. These are the failures portfolio and program management exist to prevent, which is why the case is a lesson for any large health transformation.
